utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. I heard the reason why the witness is not yet present is that the OTP asked for the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Does Your Honour want me to address that before the case is called or after?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before the case has come to an end or...? Immediately, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Regarding the subpoena or the order to have Ms. Plavsic testify, I was requested on behalf of both apparently the attorneys for Ms. Plavsic and the attorneys prosecuting the former Krajisnik and Plavsic case to ask the Court to make an order similar to the order the Court made on the recent summons, and perhaps -- well, I don't think I need to say the name. The Court recently summoned a witness and issued an order dated the 20th, a confidential order dated the 20th of December. The attorneys, both the Prosecution and the Defence representing Mrs. Plavsic, is asking for a similar order which would outline the general areas of the questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are prepared to do so. And just to clarify, because I once again read the word "subpoena" on the transcript, yesterday's press release reflected not that what has been said here in the courtroom. It was the order that Ms. Plavsic should testify as soon as practicable, but to avoid that she has to come another time to The Hague, therefore as soon as possible after her sentencing judgement. And no doubt, the parties -- we will do so, as requested. And in addition, we informed the other Trial Chamber seized with the sentencing judgement of what is planned in order to give Defence counsel and Ms. Plavsic the possibility to appear voluntarily if she so wants, maybe even before the sentencing in her case. But this is the decision of the Defence and Ms. Plavsic herself in her own case. When we discuss already practical issues, we -- I am grateful for this -- the motion of the Defence for leave to amend the witness list. I understand correctly that from this, it follows that four witnesses are exchanged. The other witnesses listed under paragraph 4, I had an opportunity to crosscheck it, they are already admitted in the list of witnesses. Correct? So that we can expect five witnesses for the next week. Are there any problems for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're not yet prepared, but we're working on it for those four witnesses. If there's a chance we may ask if it's possible to alter the order so that -- but at the moment, we're trying to just be ready in that order that the Defence proposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there should be any problem, please let us know. Without further ado, let us continue on the cross-examination of today's witness. May I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you. I get just as a judicial hint that it is appropriate to call the case. It can't be wrong. Would you please be so kind and call the case for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And at the same time, the appearances for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Markovska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're prepared to continue with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I just have to recall that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday is still valid. And may I ask the Prosecution to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam. Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the names of prisoners that you recall seeing in Omarska, people that you knew?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know a nickname, Kiki. I don't know the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's the one name that you recall, but it's correct that at the time, you recognised other persons, but ten years later --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise them, but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. These were people that you knew, but ten years later, it's difficult to remember now which persons you saw?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I still remember their faces. But I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were aware that people were being tortured in the Omarska centre. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware that they were tortured. I was aware that they were beaten. I heard them screaming, and I saw some of their injuries. So I could guess that they were beaten. Whether they were tortured, I don't know. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, you heard screams coming from the interrogation rooms; you saw people coming back badly injured from the interrogations; you saw the condition of the prisoners that you passed by; you saw the day that the delegation came and they were forced to sing. All of those things you saw. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in fact, this person you knew, the driver, Mr. Nedimovic, he was only there one day?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you said he was shocked and embarrassed by the conditions of the prisoners and threw them cigarettes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us now the incidents or the instances that you recall seeing Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by "incidents" or "instances"? What I told you was that the delegation came in cars, and the cars pulled over, and I didn't see Dr. Stakic amongst the members of that delegation. That's what I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, now I'm not talking about that. You said that you had seen Dr. Stakic before that. Is that right? Or after that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw him in Prijedor after the elections, when he was appointed vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us about how many times and under what circumstances you had seen Dr. Stakic in Prijedor, both before the time you worked in the Omarska camp and after the time you worked in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any contacts with him. I have told you that my building is across the road from the municipality building, and from my window, I could see the entrance into the municipality building. And that's where I would occasionally see Dr. Stakic as he was passing by or entering the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And what was the distance from your window to the entrance to the municipal building. Can you give us some idea?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't do that. I don't know. Somebody else maybe who is more familiar with distances would be able to give you a better answer than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's more or less across the street at an angle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not at an angle. My window was directly facing the entrance, not at an angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: From your window, by the way, is that the area below your window where the women would line up that summer, those persons wanting to leave Prijedor or find out information about the people in the camps?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't it true when you would arrive to wait for the bus -- I believe you said you waited for the bus in front of that building -- that there were lines of women, Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the only times that you saw Dr. Stakic was walking in and out of the Municipal Assembly building, from your window. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on the day that the delegation came, I'm a little confused. At that time, did you notice, did it seem unusual to you or did you make a mental note, that Dr. Stakic was not there? Was that something that occurred to you at the time, "Gee, I notice Dr. Stakic is not here"?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it didn't occur to me. I'm just telling you now whom I recognised at the time. I wasn't aware of the persons who were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, my question is, I understand you can recognise Dr. Stakic. But perhaps you can help us. Why is it you remember the absence of Dr. Stakic ten years ago from that delegation? There were many people in those cars. Why is it that you're sure that Dr. Stakic was not among the people that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you what is the characteristic of Dr. Stakic, and that's why I knew I didn't see him. Zupljanin also had something typical, and I had known him before. And I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But isn't it a fact that there probably were policemen with Mr. Drljaca, for example, his driver may have been in that delegation? But you're not sure about that, because you can't recall whether you saw him there or not, even though you can recognise him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform. There were other policemen. There was also Mrkic, Mrkic [As interpreted], and they all went to the headquarters with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think you mentioned that yesterday. Mr. Meakic was the commander of the Omarska camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Why is it that you say Mr. Meakic was not the commander of the Omarska camp? Let me make my case clear to you. It was widely known, and it was absolutely clear, that Zeljko Meakic was the commander of the Omarska camp. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Counsel is testifying that something is widely known. He should ask the questions, not to testify. And she already answered his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I already understood it that the representative of the OTP put his case to the witness, and we got a clear answer, in fact. Whether this answer is reliable or not has to be decided later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Gruban, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gruban was a reserve policeman. I believe so. Did he have a nickname? Was it Ckalja? Because I mostly knew them by their nickname. Is that the person you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, first name Momcilo, nickname Ckalja. Forgive my pronunciation, the name you --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: He was one of the persons commanding the guards when Meakic was not there. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't act as a commander. He provided security. He was a member of the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us, Mrs. Markovska, who was in charge of the Omarska camp? Who was in charge of the guards that were taking such care of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, Zeljko Meakic was the commander of the department of the police in Omarska, and he was the one who was in charge of the policemen on duty. And he put together their schedule. So there were policemen who acted as investigators; the others were providing security for the building, and that's what Zeljko Meakic did. He would put together their schedule of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. Who was in charge of the guards? Who was their commander? You mentioned he put together -- Mr. Meakic put together their schedule. Are you saying Mr. Meakic was in charge of the guards? Or are you saying that no one was in charge of the guards?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not like he was in charge. He did the same things as he did in his police department. He was the commander of the police department, and the guards did the same thing as they did in Prijedor. And I did the same thing. I typed just like I typed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Forgive me, but I do not quite understand you. Let me ask you a third time. Who was in charge, commanding the guards, at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. There was no commander. Everybody had their duty and did their job according to the schedule that was put together. So everybody knew what they were supposed to do according to that schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And if someone did not do what they were supposed to do, who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then they would have to write a statement, and then they would have to give that statement to the commander of the squad or the department commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And who would those people be? If guards did not do what they were supposed to do, who would discipline them? Who would be responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard himself would be responsible for not performing the duty. And then there was the so-called disciplinary committee or board who would hear the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was in charge of that disciplinary committee?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief who appointed members of the disciplinary committee. So it was the chief of the security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were a public security station, and our centre was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the entire time that you worked at the camp, basically from June until the camp closed, can you tell us about the reports that you typed up regarding investigations of crimes committed by Serbs against prisoners in Omarska? Did you ever type up any such reports?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any investigation of the disappearance, the torture, or the killing of prisoners at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: By the way, at the camp, did you see Mr. Knezevic; Dusko is his nickname?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you would arrive at the camp, you went through the restaurant usually. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many women prisoners did you see in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them. We just passed through. Most of them knew me. I would pass through, and I wasn't looking. I was embarrassed for being there. I was embarrassed because of the work that I had to do, because of the conditions of work. So I tried to get to my office as quickly as possible, and I took every day as it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That I can certainly understand. Can you tell us, madam, in the reports that you typed up and the interrogations, what were these women accused of doing from what you learned that caused them to be imprisoned in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I typed any of the reports concerning women. I remember the reports concerning men. That's the organisation of attacks, possession of weapons, and other things. But I can't remember exactly what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you don't recall any report indicating that any of these women had committed any offence or was a military threat to the authorities that had taken power on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On page 49 of the LiveNote of yesterday's transcript -- don't worry about the page number, I'm just saying that so the other attorneys can follow -- you were asked about a meeting following a dispatch that was brought in by Mr. Milos Jankovic. Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean there were a lot of employees, so we, from the ground floor just next to the entrance, perhaps even a bit outside. There were a lot of employees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So it wasn't in a room. It was in a corridor or outside?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The hall was full, it was crowded. There wasn't room for everyone to get in, so the door was left open, and there were people standing just outside the hall, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And were there Muslim and Croat police officers present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Everyone was there. All the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the names of the Muslim and Croat police officers who were present?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I supposed to remember? I don't even remember the Serbs. I told you already, it's a weakness I have. I don't tend to memorise names. Sometimes I can't even remember my own name. Really, I'm very bad with names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You remember the names of people you worked with for years, Muslim police officers in the police force, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sure, I do remember some. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were those persons present or you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, all the employees were present, like I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Give me the names of the Muslim police officers whose names you recall who were present at that meeting. Muslim or Croat.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you already, I can't remember any of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. How about Mr. Talundzic? Was he present?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So why didn't you remember that a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't exactly the people I worked with directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about Mr. Drago Tokmadzic, Croat, was he present?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he must have been. But I didn't really, you know, do rounds there looking at their faces and counting who was there and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In other words, it's very difficult ten years from now to remember who was present in a group of people when you're not asked for ten years who it was. It's easy to forget.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wasn't a group of people. It's a big hall full of people, crowded to capacity. We're not talking about ten people; we're talking about perhaps a hundred or more people assembled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Did you know Mirhad Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see him in -- did you know Edin Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see them in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. As I've already explained, they may have seen me, but I told you about how exactly -- the way I came in to the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And what about Sasa Karagic, did you see him, a fellow employee from the Prijedor police station, did you see him in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen him, Sasa Karagic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mirhad Mrkalj and Sasa Karagic were killed?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any of your fellow employees of Muslim or Croat ethnicity from the Prijedor police who were killed?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know who was killed? I really don't know who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I start the line of questions with two apologies. First of all, unfortunately, my LiveNote didn't work yesterday, and therefore I have the transcript before me and not the LiveNote and therefore quote from the transcript as such. And second, to the witness, because also after reading your testimony twice and three times, I wasn't really clear about some details, so therefore please understand that some questions may be repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to put S2 or the two pictures, number 1 and 2, depicted on this document, on the ELMO. While this is done, may I just for clarification, and due to the fact that the Defence has offered this information to us, is it correct, Ms. Markovska, that you're a Serb? Normally, I wouldn't ask --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- but unfortunately, in this context, we have to ask this.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you identify the two buildings on the pictures before you?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building, that's the public security station number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the other one?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could that be the building of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The image is not very clear. I really can't tell. But speaking of the model we used yesterday, I'm really very bad with these drawings and getting my bearings. Perhaps it might be easier to draw a sketch for you myself. Please don't get me wrong, but what I said about the buildings yesterday, and it was very difficult for me to really recognise them. But you have here both the SUP building and the Municipal Assembly building. I'm not really sure if this is the Municipal Assembly. I really can't see very clearly. It may as well be, but I can't say for sure. And what we said about the distances, you know, it's difficult to really see clearly. My window was at that time up on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the side we can see here on this picture, the first floor, picture number 2.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And is it -- unfortunately, we didn't have any possibility to see it ourselves. In the middle, this was your --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, here, the first one, and the second one, the one on the first floor. And from here, you can see very clearly the entrance to the Municipal Assembly. If you go there way, this is the street, and then if you take this street here, if you cross the street, you can see very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in the middle of the SUP building, this is an entrance, or is it even the main entrance, what we can see in the middle?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the entrance to the building. And this here, this is the ground floor, and then this is the police unit. This is the shift leader. And then the policemen, those who would come back from the field, and then I worked in this office here, down here. And you would take the staircase to the first floor and the second floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, the witness pointed to the windows at the right-hand side on the ground floor, and then related to her own office, to the second window seen from the main entrance to the right-hand side behind the tree. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And can you please tell us who was in the room to your left-hand side and to your right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room to the right was Ranko Mijic; and to the left, it was Zivko Jovic. I was in the one in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us come back to the time before April 30, 1992. For whom did you work at that time?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for the crime suppression department. My boss was Mr. Mijic and the inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you been specialised in certain types of crimes?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was general crime, general crime. We had the so-called economic crime and general crime. You understand about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's try again. I can understand that it's difficult to identify this from the pictures. But between the two buildings, Municipal Assembly and the SUP, is there a street or is there a park or how would you describe this?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the municipality, and here is a park. And this is where you cross the street to the building where I worked. And this is not a very large distance. I'm very bad with distances. It's always difficult for me to tell, so I often make mistakes with distances. But I can tell you for sure that there is not a big distance between these two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where would be the main entrance in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be around here, down the middle of the building. But you can't see it really in this photo. I can't see very clearly, but I think it was here, right in the middle, the main entrance hereabouts, here in front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There seems to be a car parked.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I'm saying. Yes, you can park your car here; there is some parking space outside. That's perhaps 2 or 3 metres of space, and you can leave your car right here next to the building. Right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You offered yourself to draw a sketch about the relationship of the two buildings. Could you please be so kind. May the usher give a piece of paper and a pencil to the witness that -- we tried already several times to have -- to find out where these buildings are located. So maybe you can really assist us.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the exact locations of the buildings, well, it was like this. I don't think I should draw this sketch now. I can tell you. Well, this is not exactly...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We get a good impression of this. This would be which building? The SUP?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the SUP building, and this is the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please indicate municipality building in your language, yeah. Could you mark the municipality building with an "M."

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please mark it with an "M."

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the other with an "S," please.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, my understanding is to the left-hand side of the main entrance of this building, the first floor, there was your room and you had a window to the other side, and there's the possibility to have a look on the entrance of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The estimate distance would be hundred metres, 200 metre?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am very bad with distances. I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for -- thank you, usher. We don't need this pictogram any longer. May this be the next exhibit number, J -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: J21. Admitted into evidence. When you worked in this building, you told us when you had to leave. You told us it was crime in general and economic crime. When did you hear the first time that there was planned something like the setting up of investigation centres, not limited to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, there was the attack on Prijedor, and that was in the early morning hours. It woke me up, so I didn't know what was going on. I was scared. I called the SUP to ask what was going on. They told me that Prijedor was under attack and that I shouldn't leave home before I was notified that it was safe. So I'm not sure if it was that same day or the next day, they called me and told me to come to work. They took me to work in an official police vehicle, and that's the first time they told me that I would be sent to Omarska to the investigation centre with my inspectors, because some people had been brought in there and were to be questioned by the inspectors so that criminal reports could be filed against them. That was our job. And we were told then that it would only last a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were all your colleagues, typists, investigators, secretaries asked to worked in the near future in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with my own unit, my own department. Lakic, my colleague, was sent there by state security, and they thought that the two of us would be sufficient to do the job, being the professionals that they were. But we worked every day under very strenuous conditions. So after about a month, I requested to be temporarily replaced, and then Nevenka Sikman came. Probably the people back at the station were very busy. I'm not sure what they were doing while I was over there in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But isn't it true that there were also other institutions, you call it investigation centre, aside from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while I was in Omarska, I heard of Keraterm. Trnopolje was not an investigation centre, it was a collection center. And people went there of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were colleagues of yours asked to go to Keraterm and to do the same work that you did in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that a group did go to Keraterm. But some were in Keraterm, and others were in Omarska. But not at the same time. At the beginning, everyone went to Omarska. I'm not sure when Keraterm started operating, but then at a certain time the groups split up and a small number of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever have contact with your colleagues in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there also an investigation centre in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, it's still difficult for me to understand, so therefore I have to come back to this question. When did you see yourself for the first time Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a very famous person, at least not for me. But after the elections, he became vice-president, and that's when I first found out about him being the vice-president. That was following the takeover. And then later on, he was to become president of municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been introduced to him in person?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need. How do I know? There is a colleague of mine, a person I worked with Radenko Stakic, I used to tease him, a relative of yours has just become president of the municipality, and that's why I remembered. But I don't think they were actually related, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you told us you never saw Dr. Stakic on television. You never were introduced personally to him. How could you find out that who was Dr. Stakic? A number of persons apparently are leaving and entering the building of the Municipal Assembly. How did you know the face of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a very distinctive face, Mr. President. He has a very -- he has very distinctive facial features. I've already explained why. It's because he's bald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, you told us this.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but he was only pointed out to me once, and I immediately memorised him, Stakic, Mr. President. That's later on, he became president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was my question. When was it that he was first, as you call it, pointed out to you? When was it?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the elections, as I've told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radenko Stakic, and there were other colleagues in the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I have some problems today. But I still can't understand. Was it this -- what was the name, Radenko Stakic, who introduced to you Dr. Milomir Stakic in person, that you really met Dr. Milomir Stakic in person?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not introduced me. I had heard that Mr. Stakic was vice-president of municipality, and then I teased my colleague. I used to tell him, "Now a relative of yours is the vice-president of municipality." But then he told me that they weren't related, and then he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then you don't have a connection between the face and Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean the face and Dr. Stakic? No, it was when he left the building and we were in the office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have never seen Dr. Stakic in person?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. That's exactly what I'm telling you. I saw him leave the building. This is the building he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But how can you know that was Dr. Stakic leaving the building when you were never introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't need to be introduced to know him. It didn't take a formal introduction for me to know his face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There must be any kind of introduction that you can combine a face with a certain person, that you clearly can state "I saw this person coming in, coming out." You told us just before you saw him leaving the building. When was this?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, after he became vice-president. But I can't give you the exact period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Last attempt. You saw people leaving the building of the Municipal Assembly and entering the building, a number of persons. How was it possible that you can state "I saw Dr. Stakic leaving the building of the Municipal Assembly" if you don't have a clear connection of the name. It's easy to understand that you had the name, but the combination, name and face, this is what I can't understand. How it was possible for you to identify Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, let's say I'm looking through the window. Somebody a passing by, and somebody is standing in the room with me. And that person gives me the other person's first and last names. And that person whose name I'm given has a distinctive feature, and then after that, I see that person all the time coming in and out. Sometimes I would see him leaving the municipal building towards the Rudinska building. Sometimes he would cross the street. Sometimes he would go towards the building of the Court. He was never escorted by anybody. He was just a common -- just as any other common person. He would always walk alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So your interest was focussed on Dr. Stakic, I understand?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And tell me, how is it possible that you can tell us, as you did yesterday, that you did not see Dr. Stakic entering or leaving the building of the Municipal Assembly during a certain period of time; namely, between April and September 1992? Admittedly, I couldn't tell you whom I saw or whom I did not see between April and September 1992. How is it possible that you have this clear recollection limited to April -- to the time between April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. You asked me firstly how I knew who Dr. Stakic was and how I met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, that it's quite clear for you and for all the other participants, on the official transcript, it reads "not official transcript, not corrected," page 9934, line 12, question by counsel Lukic: "Did you ever see Dr. Stakic between April and September 1992 entering the MUP building at any time?" Your answer was: "No." How is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, MUP building is not Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, right. It's not. But how is it possible? It's now a different question. How is it possible to tell that you did not see a person just in this period of time, from April to September? My question would be, did you ever see Dr. Stakic entering the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the question put to me by counsel Lukic, and my answer was no. But the question did not refer to the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. But the question counsel Lukic related to the MUP building, no doubt, was limited to April and -- to the time between April and September 1992. So my question would be, now, did you ever see Dr. Stakic entering the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So there was nothing special that you did not see Dr. Stakic entering -- not entering the MUP building between April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him entering that building. Somebody else may have, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Just for this clarification in advance, one more technical question in the order of the questions of yesterday. Is it correct that you still work in the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there any break in between since 1992?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When was this, please?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the year 2000, I retired. I was issued a retirement paper. I complained to the minister, and I received a negative answer. And then I filed an appeal with the administrative court. When I was here in 2001, I was notified that I won the case. Then I started working again. And then at the end of 2001, they -- I was retired again. Again, I complained, and then I came back to work. Again, in 2002, they wanted to retire -- put me in retirement. I complained again. I was returned to work. Again, I was -- they wanted to put me in retirement. And now I'm really fed up and tired. I don't have any more strength to fight them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear answer. When you had been ordered to go to Omarska by bus, how many people were in the bus?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many seats there were on the bus. 20 or 30, I believe. And I believe that there were some restaurant workers with us as well. They were taken to the restaurant on the same bus. They would get off, and we would continue our journey after they got off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "We," that means other typists or also investigators?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigators as well. Investigators, myself, and my colleague, the other typist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss your work or the work of the investigators during your journey to and from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't talk. The only thing I was interested in was getting home as quickly as possible. It was usually very late. We were fed up and tired, and we wanted to put the day behind us as fast as possible. We wanted to forget about the conditions of our work and the work that we were given to do as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was so bad with the work that you wanted immediately to forget about this work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One bad thing was that we were originally told that it would only last for a day or two, and it lasted much longer. And we worked long hours. Our conditions were very bad, and the inmates' conditions were even worse. And we wanted all this to be over as soon as possible so we could go back to our normal, everyday life, and to go back to working to our normal workplace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The workplace in Omarska, you shared this room with another person, or did you work alone in this room?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two of us, and we were sitting next to each other. We had two desks, two typewriters. There was a third desk for the radio set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, what is the name of your colleague you worked with and you shared the room with?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name was Slavica Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How was the work organised? Did you get some handwritten drafts or did the investigators ever dictate statements?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigators would bring us handwritten reports, and only exceptionally when there was something urgent, we would be asked to take dictations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 9.920, line 15, when you were asked by Mr. Lukic: "Did the investigators ever dictate the statements, their notes, to you directly?" You answered: "No, not to me personally, but one of my colleagues did take their notes occasionally depending on their degree of urgency." What is correct? Did they or did they not dictate to you directly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly. I've just explained that this was only exceptionally, and she would be the one to take dictations when needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your colleague taking these dictates; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was the form of the drafts? Was it in the form of questions, answers; or was it in the form of a mere report on statements of inmates of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inspectors were both from the state security and the public security, and their styles differed. But whatever they brought to us, we had to type. Sometimes it would be in the form of questions and answers; sometimes it would be in the form of statements or reports. But whatever they brought to us, we had to type, and the drafts came in all shapes and forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it foreseen that these statements should be signed by the persons who had given a statement?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements would go back to the investigators. What they did with them, I don't know. Whether they gave them to somebody to sign them or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you got such a request to type a statement, be it in the form of question and answer or a report only, before April 30, wasn't it a custom that under the entire text, there was space for the signatures of the investigator and the person who gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But when we were there, we were told not to put anything like that. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you were asked about superiors of, for example, Mr. Jesic and others. That we don't forget it, you were not asked who was the superior to Mr. Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably somebody from Banja Luka. He was an officer in the army, so I don't know. I would only see him occasionally. Sometimes he would come to our office, but I didn't have anything to do with the army whatsoever. I sometimes -- I didn't even communicate with my own bosses, let alone him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you had never to type anything on behalf of this military personnel. Correct? There was a distinction between police and military, and you had never to type anything from persons working together with Mr. Majstorovic, subordinates of him? Or was it also possible that --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you at one point that we had inspectors for -- from all over the place, from the state security, from the public security, from the military security. They would sign the statements. They had their nicknames, their pseudonyms, and I would sometimes not know where -- who they were affiliated with, which branch of security they were affiliated with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of you told us yesterday that you brought parcels, sometimes parcels to Omarska. What was the reason for this? Did you know anybody there who you believed that it would be necessary that these persons get parcels?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took parcels on behalf of Nedzija Fazlic, whose husband was there. And there was a need. Everybody needed something. The majority of those who were in Omarska found a way to have things brought to them. And I did that on several occasions, whenever she asked me to do her that favour, I would take something to her husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzija Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nadzija or Nedzija Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nadzija or Nedzija, it's just one letter. I believe it's an A, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have a good relationship with her or her husband?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we just worked together. We were never really close. I never socialised with any of my colleagues. I had my own family who needed me after work. And I had very little time after work to spend with my family, let alone hang out with any of my colleagues from work. So I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was the only person who received parcels from you, or were there also other persons?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only person who received parcels from me. But there were other people. There was another colleague of mine who took parcels to Omarska. Some of my colleagues, inspectors, also took parcels. Policemen as well very often took things to Omarska. Things would be brought to Omarska in different way, by different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever have the idea, having worked for the criminal police in Prijedor for a long period of time, to bring parcels to inmates in Prijedor, being arrested for crimes?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean when you say "in Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us yesterday and today in the beginning that previously, you worked on ordinary crimes, economic crimes, and I think in this connection, there were also persons arrested. Did you ever have the idea to bring a parcel to an inmate based on such an arrest warrant for economic crime?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have a detention unit. And while investigation was going on and while these people were kept there, they were given food and stuff. And we could only keep them for three days, for the purpose of investigation. And after that, we would send them to Banja Luka. So nobody was actually detained in Prijedor for a longer period of time. And if they needed something like coffee or cigarettes, that's what we would give them while they were detained in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to finalise this, before the break, how many times did you bring parcels to Ms. Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was four times or more, I can't really remember. She would wait for me in front of the bus whenever she wanted me to take something there. I would take it from her, and I would take it to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What ethnicity was the family Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that there was a number of lists, some short lists, some longer lists, sometimes even pages, you had to type containing names of inmates. And you -- can you identify by the names whether there was a majority of Muslims and Croats on these lists?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see names of former colleagues, policemen or neighbours of yours or other persons you knew from Prijedor, on these lists?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- there must have been, but I can't remember any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's easy to understand. Ten years later, I myself would not be able to recollect the names. I have the same problem as you have. But is it true that at that time, you could think "This is a neighbour, former neighbour of mine, this is a former colleague of mine" on the list? Is this true that this happened sometimes?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did you understand why it was necessary to detain these persons you knew?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand. I didn't know, but I suppose that those who detained them knew why they did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's have a break now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the usher to put Document S15-18 on the ELMO, please. Madam Markovska, yesterday you told us where your office was located and where the restaurant room was. Can you please be so kind to show us on this picture from where the delegation and the cars came.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They passed here, this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The cars as such entered the -- this area? And they did not stay outside the area.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. I mean, the vehicles with the delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apropos, the delegation, was it only once there was a delegation?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please once again with the pointer point to the restaurant room from where you had the possibility to see the delegation.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't in the restaurant; it was in the largest room where we took breakfast. That was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it was during the time you took breakfast the delegation arrived?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I explained yesterday, we knew that the delegation would be arriving, and through our window we could see, we could observe their arrival outside. And you could hear people singing. As my colleague was a bit more curious than I was, and she used to move about a bit more, she said "Let's just go there and look at them." Once we were back in our office, the door was open, and they passed -- they entered here. They took this entrance. They went up the stairs and went to the staff room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So what time of the day was it when this group of delegation arrived?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the morning hours. I don't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it close to breakfast or close to lunch?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was between breakfast and lunch, I think, but I can't say with any degree of precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to go into these details, but did you take breakfast, lunch, and dinner in this restaurant room?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we only had breakfast here. But lunch, which was lunch and dinner at the same time, that was after we returned, the restaurant where they prepared the food for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was outside the Omarska area --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The restaurant was called "Separation." Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, you had already finished breakfast, went back to your office; then you were aware that a delegation would come, and went back to the room where you had breakfast before, but it was still in the morning. Is this correct? Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I can't give you the exact time, but we knew that the delegation would arrive on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But to be -- we have to be precise here. To the best of your recollection, it was, as you said, between breakfast and lunch.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should suppose so. But I can't tell you anything more precise than that. Breakfast was sometimes at 10.00, sometimes at 11.00, sometimes even as late as at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And then you got your meal. It might be of assistance to have a look on the video. I think until now, it has only a 65 ter number, 807. May we please see only one very short clip of 65 ter number 807. And may I ask Madam Registrar to crosscheck whether this was already admitted into evidence or not. Yes, please play the video now. If you want to comment on something, please say stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "SPEAKER: ... also being denied access to Omarska, hidden until now from the world. We were not allowed to follow them to their living accommodation --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Can you identify this building? If you please could wind a little bit back that we can see the entire first building. Stop. Stop here. Can you see now where is the room where you worked and the room where you had breakfast?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room where we had breakfast, you can't see it in this picture. You can't see it from this particular angle, because it's inside the building, and this was the office where we worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you point to the room where you --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps it's this one here. I'm talking about the room where we had breakfast, but I can't see very clearly. I'm not sure. But I do know that you passed through a corridor, and then the last room on this side of the building, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please use the pointer.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. What am I supposed to point at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Sorry, this was my mistake. You pointed in the direction to the right-hand side above the car standing there. But the first floor, would this be the room where you had breakfast or --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's actually behind, behind over there. I'm not sure if the window was here. But this is really difficult to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Then let's turn back to the entire building. Thank you for offering this other picture. Let's turn back to the video, please. Could we please see from the video unit the picture of the building on the video, please. May we have the video once again, that what we saw a moment before. Here, your own office room, could you identify your own office room.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I make a suggestion. I don't know if this would work, but is it possible to have the witness, just for this purpose, sit where the Registrar is use and the monitor and counsel and I can stand behind and we can all see what she is pointing at, Your Honours can see what she is pointing at. Use the microphone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is possible to use the microphones. We see a number of rooms on the first floor. Did your office have to this side of the building, was there a window to this side of the building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was here, but I'm not sure which room it was. I'm not sure where the toilet was. And then just next to the toilet was where my office was located. But I'm not sure if it's these windows here, this row of windows, or another one. But I really can't be sure. I've tried to explain as well as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I understand that -- please, let the video as it is. That when the delegation arrived, you left your office room, maybe heading to this side, and went to the other room where you --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, this other side. This is not where I was. We went to the other one over there where I said we used to have breakfast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. So you left your office and went to the room where you had breakfast.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And can you exclude that part of the group went in front of the house we see now on the video before us, and another part of the group you saw there from this breakfast room?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which group exactly you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are discussing --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- the appearance of a delegation, and the question is --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Can you exclude that you saw only a part of the group from this breakfast room, and another part of the group, which would be the testimony of another witness, went along this side we can see now on the video in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they all came this way and went out where I told you. They passed that section; they took the main entrance, and then they went straight to the main room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Main entrance this would be from the direction we are sitting now in front of the building, and the main entrance would be directly --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, they had to pass the restaurant on their way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you exclude that some cars remained outside this area of Omarska, and some of the dignitaries went by foot the one or other direction?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't find it likely. You can see clearly from this room. We could watch them arrive, the entire delegation. I don't believe that any of them would have walked. I don't find it likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us that you heard people singing. Did you know where these - I think it were inmates - were located? Because I think the intention of singing is to give a salute to the delegation. Wouldn't this be true? Could you see the inmates singing from your breakfast room?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you see inmates singing and preparing for the appearance of this delegation from your office room before the delegation arrived?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I leaned out the window, yes, I could see, but that's not what I did. They were here, next to this wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So they were lined up in front of this house we can see before us. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what kind of songs did they sing?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sang Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Even though they were Muslims and Croats, they sung Chetnik songs. They were forced to sing these songs?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were forced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did the group, the delegation, ever pass these lined-up inmates? Because only this would make sense, that they clearly can hear and see what is going on.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't pass them, but on their way in, yes, I think they could see them. That was the point of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us leave it with the video -- with this video. Maybe we come back to another one. But we should not forget, if there are no objections, to admit this video with the 65 ter number 807 as J22. You told us yesterday that you typed lists of inmates. Were there several categories of inmates?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we typed the lists, no, there weren't any different categories. But later on, I heard that there had been different categories. Now who was in charge of defining the categories, I really didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what are the different categories?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard they had the first, second, and third categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was the underlying reason for having three categories? What did it mean, for example, to be put into category 1?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose those would have been persons who had taken part in the organisation of the attack and the attack itself on Prijedor, and the attack against the army. I suppose those would have been the persons included in group 1. Group 2 were probably persons in possession of weapons. And group 3, those who had nothing in particular. And most of persons categorised as belonging to group 3 were later released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Released directly or via another, call it, investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they were released exactly, I know that they were released. Now who released them, I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever later, it's now ten years ago, speak with your neighbours or other citizens of Prijedor about this categorisation, and did you ever speak with people who survived the Omarska camp or investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I be allowed to add something? You asked me about my ethnic background, and I told you. But I never looked at people as belonging to different ethnic groups. The only thing that matter to me was what kind of person you were, and even in my family, there are a whole lot of mixed marriages. And even after the war, I still have friends who are Muslim or Croats. We sometimes have coffee together. We talk over the cup of coffee we share. If you're a good person, you're just a good person. And even during the war, it was the same. I believe that I was -- I managed to stay a good person, too. And whenever someone appealed to me for help, regardless of their ethnic background, I helped wherever I could. It's still the same today, and I intend to stay that way. Before the war, I didn't even know who was a Croat and who was a Serb. Muslims had particular -- very distinctive names, so you could tell a Muslim from the other people. I was a member of the party back then, before the war. But I will never be a member of any other party. I'm not really into politics. I just do my job. That's all. I used to see a lot of Kiki who was later in Omarska. He would always greet me. I saw Vahid later on, afterwards, when the whole thing was over, and he also said hello. There may have been people who had a different view of me, but then again, those people who see me in a different light probably won't say hello when they pass me on the street. I think I was the same person before the war, during the war, and after the war. I have always stayed the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, no doubt, this is the way we should look on each other irrespective of the background, be it the political, ethnical, or other background. And I appreciate your special comments on this. But we have to find out what happened at that time in Omarska and in other camps --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- and you already told us that on the basis of the names, you could identify that there were numerous if not the majority of the inmates of the lists you had to type of Muslim ethnicity. It's a shame that one has to make this distinction, but apparently at that time some superiors decided that this should be necessary. Looking back -- I already touched upon this issue on the statements, the results of the interrogations -- did you always see that there was an alleged crime as you were acquainted in the past that, for example, to a certain extent you worked in the area that we are working now when you were working for the criminal police, but in the beginning, there was an offence mentioned, and then later on the person was warned that a person has a right to remain silent and all these warnings, the right to have defence counsel, was all this included in the statements you had to type?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't part of it. Before the war, it wasn't really common practice. That's after the law was amended. If a person is brought in, if any person is brought in, they have a right to legal assistance and to remain silent. But it wasn't like that before the war. It was not envisaged by the law. It was only after the person receives a decision on detention, then this state that he has a right to legal assistance. And after the case is forwarded to the judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the inmates in Omarska? Did they have the same rights? Did you ever see defence counsel working on behalf of the inmates? Did you ever see something like these admonitions in the statements or question/answer you had to type?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just explained during the war, and before the war for that matter, this was not part of our law. The whole time they were there, no criminal reports were ever filed against them, and they were still being investigated. It was only after a criminal report has been filed that you can -- then you detain the person, and it's only then that the person is entitled to receive legal assistance. And the reports only contained what they had previously stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But to be very concrete, did the report and the line of questions start with the concrete alleged offence?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say that, you mean whether that was in the statement? No, that wasn't in the statement. The article was not mentioned; the alleged act was not mentioned. This is something that would be part of a criminal report, and these initial statements are enclosures to the possible future criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this concrete answer. May we take the opportunity and if you could be so kind and follow the video we can see now on our screen. Could the usher please be so kind and change the screen of Madam Markovska. Could this video be played. This would be, then, J23, the former 806, 65 ter number. Could the video please be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. May we please stop the video. Rewind it a little bit back. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's who, please?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And wind a little bit further. If you can recognise a person, please tell us. And then a little bit, wind it back, please. Do you recognise this room? Please wind back again, further. Stop, please. This was the main entrance to Omarska. Correct? Can you identify this?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. The image is moving. That's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could move on a little bit that it becomes more clear. Would this be another view, another perspective on the building you were at that time when the delegation appeared?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. I can't see clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's leave it with this video. And then may we finally have a look on Exhibit S157, the next video, please. Can you move it a little bit forward and backwards. Can you identify the persons sitting here. And can you please tell us who are the four men sitting on the left-hand side. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10010 to 10016.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic, Mico Kovacevic, and I believe that the third one is Drljaca, and I can't see the fourth person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the video be played a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Did you ever see yourself Dr. Stakic in uniform as we could see it on the video here?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember ever seeing him in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see the late Dr. Kovacevic or Simo Drljaca entering the building of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca, I don't know. I didn't see him at the time while I was in Omarska. But later on, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the time before, especially in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come that your recollection is focussed in this way on Dr. Stakic? Was he such a prominent person, or what was the reason that, to the best of your recollection, you can testify today that you saw Dr. Stakic several times leaving the municipal building, because you could see him from your window as you indicated, but not the other ones? How is this possible? Was he the most responsible person? Or what -- I still want to --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What's the reason that you focussed this way on Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
